section.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Staging Investigations for Your Cancer Type
section.intro: Staging investigations confirm how far a cancer has spread and guide treatment planning. These FAQs explain the common tests, why they differ by cancer type, and what international patients should prepare.

items.q: What are staging investigations for cancer?
items.a: Staging investigations are tests that determine how large a cancer is and whether it has spread beyond its original site. They typically include imaging scans, blood tests, biopsies, and sometimes surgical assessment. The exact combination depends on your cancer type, location, and symptoms. Accurate staging helps the oncology team choose the right treatment and estimate prognosis. Which tests you need should be decided by your treating specialists after reviewing your case.

items.q: Why do staging tests differ for each cancer type?
items.a: Staging tests differ because each cancer spreads in its own pattern and to specific organs. For example, breast cancer often needs imaging of bones, liver, and lungs, while colon cancer focuses on the abdomen and pelvis. The tests are chosen to check the sites where a particular cancer is most likely to travel. Your required investigations depend on cancer type, stage, biomarker profile, symptoms, and specialist review, and should be confirmed by your oncology team.

items.q: What is the TNM staging system?
items.a: The TNM system is the most widely used method for describing how far a cancer has spread. T describes the size or extent of the primary tumour, N shows whether nearby lymph nodes are involved, and M indicates whether the cancer has spread to distant organs. Staging tests provide the information needed to assign each value. The final stage combines these into groups from early to advanced, and interpretation should be done by your treating team.

items.q: How is imaging used in cancer staging?
items.a: Imaging shows the size, location, and possible spread of a cancer without surgery. Common scans include CT, MRI, ultrasound, PET-CT, and bone scans, each chosen for what it shows best. CT and PET-CT often assess distant spread, MRI gives detail for brain, spine, or pelvic tumours, and ultrasound helps view soft tissue and lymph nodes. The imaging you need depends on cancer type and should be selected by your radiology and oncology team.

groups.title: Common Tests and the Staging Process

items.q: What blood tests are done during cancer staging?
items.a: Blood tests during staging assess overall health and may include tumour markers linked to specific cancers. Examples include CA-125 for ovarian cancer, PSA for prostate cancer, AFP and beta-hCG for certain testicular and liver cancers, and LDH in lymphoma. Blood counts, kidney, and liver function are also checked to guide treatment safety. Tumour markers support but do not replace imaging and biopsy, and results should be interpreted by your oncology team.

items.q: Is a biopsy part of staging investigations?
items.a: A biopsy confirms cancer by examining a tissue sample under a microscope and is central to accurate staging. It identifies the cancer type, grade, and often biomarkers that guide treatment. In some cancers, lymph nodes are biopsied to check for spread, such as a sentinel node biopsy in breast cancer or melanoma. Whether and where a biopsy is needed depends on your cancer type and specialist assessment by your treating pathology and surgical team.

items.q: When is a PET-CT scan needed for staging?
items.a: A PET-CT scan is often used when doctors need to check for cancer spread throughout the body in one study. It highlights areas of high metabolic activity that may indicate cancer, and is commonly used in lymphoma, lung cancer, and some head and neck cancers. It is not required for every cancer or every stage. Whether a PET-CT is appropriate depends on your cancer type, stage, and the questions your oncology team needs answered.

items.q: How long does the staging process usually take?
items.a: The staging process usually takes from a few days to a couple of weeks, depending on which tests are needed and how quickly results become available. Some patients complete imaging and blood tests within days, while biopsy analysis, biomarker testing, or specialist review can add time. Delays may occur if additional scans are needed. Your exact timeline depends on your hospital, test availability, and case complexity, and should be discussed with your treating team.

items.q: Do I need to repeat staging tests after treatment starts?
items.a: Staging tests are sometimes repeated to check how a cancer responds to treatment, a process called restaging. Scans and blood tests may be done partway through or after therapy to measure changes in tumour size or spread. This helps the team decide whether to continue, adjust, or change treatment. How often restaging is done depends on your cancer type, treatment plan, and specialist judgement, and should be guided by your treating oncology team.

items.q: How much do cancer staging investigations cost?
items.a: The cost of staging investigations varies widely depending on which tests are needed, the country, and the hospital. Basic blood tests and ultrasound are usually low cost, while PET-CT, MRI, and molecular biomarker testing are more expensive. A full staging workup may combine several tests. Final costs depend on your diagnosis, the number and type of scans, laboratory fees, and hospital pricing, and should be confirmed with the treating centre before proceeding.

items.q: What reports should I bring for a staging review or second opinion?
items.a: For a staging review or second opinion, bring your biopsy and pathology reports, imaging scans with the actual images on disk, blood test and tumour marker results, and any biomarker or genetic testing reports. A summary of your diagnosis, previous treatments, and current medications is also helpful. Complete and recent reports allow specialists to assess your case accurately. Your treating team can advise which documents are most important for your specific cancer type.

items.q: Are advanced staging tests available in India?
items.a: Advanced staging tests, including PET-CT, high-field MRI, and molecular biomarker testing, are available at many major cancer centres in India. Availability can vary between cities and hospitals, and some specialised tests may only be offered at larger referral centres. Turnaround times and costs also differ by facility. Whether a specific test is suitable and where it is best performed depends on your cancer type and should be confirmed with the treating hospital.

items.q: Which staging tests require special preparation?
items.a: Some staging tests need preparation to give accurate results. PET-CT usually requires fasting and controlled blood sugar, contrast-enhanced CT and MRI may need you to avoid food for a few hours, and certain scans require normal kidney function before contrast. You may be asked to pause specific medications. Instructions vary by test and hospital, so follow the exact guidance given by your imaging centre and confirm any preparation steps with your treating team.

items.q: What is molecular or biomarker testing in staging?
items.a: Molecular or biomarker testing examines the cancer's genes and proteins to guide targeted and personalised treatment. It can identify markers such as HER2 in breast cancer, EGFR in lung cancer, or PD-L1 for immunotherapy decisions. While not part of anatomical staging, it is increasingly done alongside it to plan therapy. Whether biomarker testing is appropriate depends on your cancer type, stage, and available tissue, and should be recommended by your treating oncology team.

items.q: Are staging investigations part of clinical trial eligibility?
items.a: Staging investigations are often required to assess whether a patient qualifies for a clinical trial. Trials usually need up-to-date imaging, biopsy, and biomarker results to confirm cancer type, stage, and measurable disease. Eligibility is decided only after medical records are reviewed and the investigator assesses inclusion and exclusion criteria. Meeting the staging requirements does not guarantee enrolment or benefit, and suitability must be confirmed by the trial team after full evaluation.

items.q: What if my staging results are unclear or inconclusive?
items.a: When staging results are unclear, doctors may recommend additional or repeat tests to reach a confident conclusion. This can include further imaging, a repeat or additional biopsy, or specialist review of scans and pathology. A second opinion is also reasonable in uncertain cases. Inconclusive results are not unusual and do not necessarily indicate advanced disease. The next steps depend on your cancer type and findings, and should be guided carefully by your treating oncology team.

items.q: Can I complete some staging tests in my home country before travelling?
items.a: Many patients complete initial staging tests, such as blood work, basic imaging, and biopsy, in their home country before travelling for treatment. Sharing these reports early can speed up planning and reduce repeated tests abroad. However, the receiving hospital may still repeat certain scans to confirm findings or meet its own standards. Which tests can be done locally and which must be redone depends on the treating centre and should be confirmed in advance.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with staging investigations for their cancer type?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organise medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centres, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. This can make it easier to arrange the right staging tests and share results with the treating team. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health, and no specific test outcome or access can be guaranteed.
